results.summary: This design is a driver for a hexagonal charlieplexed LED matrix with columns of 3-4-5-4-3 pixels. It accepts serial data on ui[0] while ui[1] is low, loading the pattern column-wise, and then drives the matrix through five bidirectional pins when ui[1] is high. Testing requires an external charlieplexed LED display (or individual LEDs) connected to the uio pins, with the clock pulsed at 100 Hz or more. The project is notable for targeting a non-rectangular charlieplexed matrix and is implemented in Wokwi.

This project is a placeholder created during a Hackaday workshop, with no functional description provided. The documentation explicitly states that the author refuses to describe how it works or how to test it. No pins or external hardware are specified. As a result, there is insufficient information to determine the design's purpose or capabilities.

This is a default Tiny Tapeout project that displays three segments lighting up on a 7-segment display. It is intended to be used as a template for building more complex 7-segment projects. No specific inputs or outputs are documented beyond the display segments. The design is a starting point for beginners and was created at a Hackaday workshop.

This design simulates rolling a dice, displaying the result on a 7-segment display. Pulling input 0 high causes the dice to roll, and releasing it stops the roll. It requires an external 7-segment display connected to outputs 0-6 and a button connected to input 0. Silicon tests confirm it works, though the author notes that using the microswitch to stop the roll is a bit annoying.

This project is titled 'Some_LEDs' and described as 'Nothing special'. The documentation states that the author does not yet know how it works and that testing involves connecting the right things. No pins or external hardware are specified. There is insufficient information to determine the design's functionality or purpose.

This is the example project from the Wokwi Hackaday Europe workshop, with no modifications. It displays segments on a 7-segment display based on the states of switches 0-7. Testing involves flipping the switches to turn on the corresponding segments. The design serves as a starting point for workshop participants.

This project was designed during a Hackaday workshop, but the documentation consists only of 'TODO' placeholders for how it works, how to test, and external hardware. No pins or functional details are provided. There is insufficient information to determine what the design does.

This design shows two animations on a 7-segment display: alternating letters F and H, or a rotation animation. It divides a 10 kHz clock input based on input 7 and uses input 0 to select the mode, input 1 for blinking the dot, input 5 to pause, and input 6 for debug. Testing requires applying a 10 kHz clock and observing the display; silicon tests confirm it works correctly. The project was created during the Hackaday Conference 2024.

This design implements two pseudorandom number generators (PRNGs) using scan flip-flops and XOR gates, one with and one without a hardware trojan. It includes scan chain inputs for setting the PRNG state and an external trigger for the trojan, with outputs for both PRNGs and test points for inverters. Testing involves providing a clock, setting the scan inputs, toggling scan enable, and using a pattern generator and logic analyzer. The project is notable for demonstrating a hardware trojan in a PRNG context.

This design tests servo signals by lighting up eight LEDs according to the pulse width of the input signal. A 1 ms pulse (0 degrees) lights no LEDs, while a 2 ms pulse (180 degrees) lights all eight. It requires an external 4 kHz clock, eight LEDs with resistors, and a servo signal on input 0. The design uses flip-flops to process the servo signal and is implemented in Wokwi.
